title: Server-Side Rendering (SSR)
summary: **Server-Side Rendering (SSR)** renders a route's HTML on the server **on every request**, so each visitor gets fully-formed, data-filled HTML tailored to that moment — ideal for personalized or always-fresh pages that still need SEO.

subtopics.title: What SSR actually does
subtopics.explanation: On each incoming request the server runs your Server Component, fetches data, renders React to HTML, and streams it to the browser. The user sees real content immediately and crawlers index it, but the server does work for every single request. In the App Router this happens automatically whenever a route reads request-specific data.

subtopics.title: Opting in with no-store fetch
subtopics.explanation: The simplest way to force SSR for a route is to make its data fetch uncacheable. A fetch with cache: 'no-store' is re-run on every request, which opts the whole route into dynamic (server-per-request) rendering. Use this when the data genuinely changes between requests.

subtopics.title: Dynamic functions (cookies, headers, searchParams)
subtopics.explanation: Reading request-only data — cookies(), headers(), draftMode(), or the searchParams prop — depends on the incoming request, so Next.js cannot pre-render the page at build time and automatically switches it to SSR. This is how personalized pages (per-user content based on a session cookie) become dynamic.
subtopics.example:
import { cookies } from 'next/headers';
const session = cookies().get('session')?.value;

subtopics.title: force-dynamic route config
subtopics.explanation: You can opt an entire route segment into SSR explicitly with a route segment config export, regardless of how its fetches are cached. This is useful when you want a guarantee that the route is always dynamic, or to document the intent for reviewers.
subtopics.example:
// top of app/dashboard/page.tsx
export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic';

subtopics.title: Pros: SEO, freshness, security
subtopics.explanation: SSR sends complete HTML so crawlers see real content (great SEO) and users see data on first paint. Because rendering and data access happen on the server, secrets and tokens never reach the client, and each response reflects the latest data — perfect for personalized or rapidly-changing pages.
subtopics.example: // Secrets stay server-side; HTML arrives data-filled and indexable

subtopics.title: Cons: TTFB and server cost
subtopics.explanation: Because the server renders per request, time-to-first-byte is slower than CDN-served static pages, and you pay for compute on every visit. Under heavy traffic SSR routes need scaling. The fix is to reserve SSR for genuinely dynamic routes and use SSG/ISR for everything cacheable.
subtopics.example: // Per-request render = higher TTFB + per-visit server cost

subtopics.title: SSR vs SSG
subtopics.explanation: SSG renders once at build and serves frozen HTML from a CDN — fastest and cheapest but stale until rebuild. SSR renders fresh per request — always current but slower and costlier. Choose SSR only when content must reflect the current request (per-user, per-moment); otherwise prefer SSG or ISR.
subtopics.example: SSG: build once, serve forever | SSR: render every request

foundations.overview: Server-Side Rendering produces a route's HTML on the server for each incoming request, embedding live data into the markup before it reaches the browser. In the Next.js App Router, a route becomes server-rendered (dynamic) the moment it reads request-specific data or opts out of caching, giving you fresh, personalized, SEO-friendly pages at the cost of per-request server work.
foundations.formalDefinition: SSR (dynamic rendering) is the strategy where a route's HTML is generated on the server at request time, using data that may differ per request, rather than at build time. In Next.js it is triggered by uncached fetches, dynamic functions (cookies/headers/searchParams), or an explicit force-dynamic segment config.
foundations.whyItMatters: SSR is the correct strategy for content that must be current or user-specific while remaining indexable and fast to first paint. Knowing precisely what makes a route dynamic — and what it costs — is a core Next.js competency and a frequent interview topic.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture a chef cooking each dish to order: every customer (request) gets a freshly made plate (HTML) reflecting today's ingredients (live data) and their preferences (cookies/session). It's fresh and bespoke, but the kitchen works for every order, so it's slower and more expensive than serving pre-made meals (SSG).
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser receives complete, data-filled HTML it can paint immediately for good first contentful paint, then downloads JavaScript to hydrate it into an interactive React tree. Unlike CSR, there is no blank loading state before content appears.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A logged-in account page that greets the user by name, a personalized feed, a checkout page reflecting live inventory and prices, or a dashboard whose data must be current on every load.
foundations.businessImpact: Fresh, personalized pages that still rank in search drive engagement and conversion; but because SSR consumes server compute per request, over-using it inflates hosting bills, so right-sizing protects margins at scale.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Engineers must understand exactly which APIs make a route dynamic (cookies, headers, no-store) to avoid accidentally server-rendering static content — a common cause of slow, expensive apps. SSR also keeps data-access logic and secrets safely on the server.
foundations.performanceImpact: SSR adds per-request latency (the server fetches data and renders before responding), raising TTFB versus CDN-served static pages, and it consumes server CPU/memory per visit. Streaming and caching mitigate but do not eliminate this cost.
commonUseCases: Personalized pages that read a session/auth cookie
Always-fresh data like live prices, inventory, or feeds
Pages whose output depends on request headers or search params
Dashboards and account pages that must reflect the latest state per load

commonMisconceptions.myth: SSR caches the rendered HTML by default so it's as fast as static.
commonMisconceptions.reality: SSR re-renders on every request by design; it is not CDN-cached unless you add caching/ISR. Its TTFB is inherently higher than pre-built static HTML.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You must write a special function (like getServerSideProps) to do SSR in the App Router.
commonMisconceptions.reality: In the App Router there's no getServerSideProps. A route becomes SSR implicitly from uncached fetches or dynamic functions, or explicitly via export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'.

visualExplorer.title: An SSR request, step by step
visualExplorer.caption: Follow a single request from browser to interactive page when a route is server-rendered.

config.intro: Walk through what happens on the server (and then the browser) for one SSR request.

steps.name: Request arrives
steps.detail: The browser requests the route. Because the route reads request-specific data (or is force-dynamic), Next.js renders it on the server for THIS request rather than serving a pre-built file.

steps.name: Read request data
steps.detail: The server reads dynamic inputs — cookies(), headers(), or searchParams — to personalize the response (e.g. the current user's session).

steps.name: Fetch live data
steps.detail: An uncached fetch (cache: 'no-store') pulls the latest data from APIs/databases, guaranteeing the response reflects the current moment.

steps.name: Render HTML
steps.detail: The server runs the Server Component, renders React to fully-formed HTML with the data embedded, and streams it back. Secrets stay server-side.

steps.name: Paint + hydrate
steps.detail: The browser paints the complete HTML immediately (good FCP/SEO), then downloads JS to hydrate it into an interactive React app.

interactiveExamples.title: What 'fresh per request' feels like (runnable)
interactiveExamples.explanation: SSR re-evaluates data on every request. This client demo simulates that by computing a fresh value each time you 'request' the page — the analog of the server re-rendering per request. (In Next this logic runs on the server.)
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A timestamp that updates every time you click 'Simulate a new request', mimicking per-request server rendering.

interactiveExamples.title: Three ways to make a route SSR (illustrative)
interactiveExamples.explanation: In the App Router a route becomes server-rendered via an uncached fetch, a dynamic function, or force-dynamic. This App renders that real Next.js code as text — it's illustrative, since these run on the server in a real app.

codeLab.title: Classify: dynamic (SSR) or static?
codeLab.instructions: For each route description, decide whether Next.js will render it dynamically (SSR) and why. Edit the component to fill in your answers, then Run. (A page reading a session cookie; a page with a plain cached fetch; a page using cache:'no-store'; a page exporting force-dynamic.)
codeLab.expectedOutput: Your dynamic-vs-static call for each route with a reason.
hints: A route is dynamic if it reads request-only data or opts out of caching.
Default fetches are cached -> static; no-store / cookies / headers / force-dynamic -> SSR.

debuggingLab.title: Personalized page shows the wrong (cached) user
debuggingLab.symptom: A page that should greet the logged-in user sometimes shows a different user's name, because it was statically cached at build time instead of rendered per request.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The default fetch is cached, so Next.js pre-renders this page at build time and serves the same HTML to everyone. Because the user identity depends on the request (the session cookie), the page MUST be dynamic. Relying on a cached fetch for per-user data leaks one user's data to others.
commonMistakes: Fetching per-user data with a default (cached) fetch, making the page static.
Forgetting that reading the session must happen per request via a dynamic function.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make the route render per request: read the session via cookies() (a dynamic function) and/or use cache: 'no-store' for the user fetch.

theory.question: What is Server-Side Rendering in Next.js and when should you use it?
theory.directAnswer: SSR renders a route's HTML on the server for every request, embedding live, possibly per-user data before sending it to the browser. Use it when content must be fresh on each load or personalized (reads cookies/headers) while still needing SEO and fast first paint. In the App Router a route becomes SSR via an uncached fetch, a dynamic function, or export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic' — there's no getServerSideProps.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A dynamic rendering strategy where HTML is produced on the server at request time using request-specific data.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Some content can't be pre-built because it depends on the current request (the logged-in user, the latest data, request headers).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Next.js runs the Server Component per request, reads dynamic inputs and uncached data, renders React to HTML, streams it, and the browser then hydrates it.

theory.whyImportant: SSR is essential for personalized and always-fresh pages and is a core App Router concept; misusing it (or accidentally triggering it) directly affects performance and cost.
theory.realWorldExample: A logged-in account page greets the user by name and shows their latest orders — it reads the session cookie and fetches with no-store, so it renders per request.

nestedTopics.title: Dynamic functions
nestedTopics.explanation: cookies(), headers(), draftMode(), and searchParams depend on the request and force dynamic rendering.

nestedTopics.title: Uncached fetch
nestedTopics.explanation: fetch(url, { cache: 'no-store' }) re-runs each request and opts the route into SSR.

nestedTopics.title: force-dynamic
nestedTopics.explanation: A route segment config that explicitly makes the whole route render dynamically.

followUps.question: How do you trigger SSR for a route in the App Router?
followUps.answer: Use an uncached fetch (cache: 'no-store'), read a dynamic function like cookies()/headers(), or export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic' at the top of the segment.

followUps.question: Is there a getServerSideProps in the App Router?
followUps.answer: No. That's a Pages Router API. In the App Router, async Server Components plus caching/dynamic-function choices decide rendering.

theory.question: What are the trade-offs of SSR compared with SSG, and what are its main costs?
theory.directAnswer: SSR gives fresh, personalized, secure, SEO-friendly HTML but at the cost of higher TTFB and per-request server compute, since the server renders on every visit. SSG renders once at build and serves frozen HTML from a CDN — far faster and cheaper but stale until rebuild. So SSR's strengths (freshness, personalization) are exactly SSG's weaknesses, and vice versa; you pick SSR only when content truly depends on the request.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A comparison of per-request rendering (SSR) versus build-time rendering (SSG).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Each strategy optimizes a different axis: SSR optimizes freshness, SSG optimizes speed/cost.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: SSR fetches and renders per request (latency + compute); SSG pre-builds and serves from CDN (instant but static).

theory.whyImportant: Choosing wrong — SSR-ing static content — is a leading cause of slow, expensive Next.js apps, and the trade-off is a classic interview discriminator.
theory.realWorldExample: A marketing homepage served as SSR has poor TTFB and high cost; switching it to SSG makes it CDN-fast and nearly free, while a personalized dashboard correctly stays SSR.

nestedTopics.title: TTFB
nestedTopics.explanation: SSR's server work per request raises time-to-first-byte versus CDN-served static HTML.

nestedTopics.title: Server cost
nestedTopics.explanation: Every SSR request consumes compute, so SSR scales with traffic and server capacity.

nestedTopics.title: Security
nestedTopics.explanation: SSR keeps data access and secrets on the server, never shipping them to the client.

followUps.question: How can you reduce SSR's TTFB cost?
followUps.answer: Stream the response (Suspense), cache cacheable sub-fetches, and consider ISR or Partial Prerendering so only the truly dynamic parts render per request.

scenario.question: Your personalized dashboard is correctly per-user but its TTFB is too high under load. How do you keep personalization while improving performance?
scenario.directAnswer: Keep the personalized parts SSR but shrink the dynamic work: stream the page with Suspense so the static shell paints immediately while personalized sections fill in, cache the sub-fetches that aren't user-specific, and push purely interactive bits to small Client Components. If parts are shareable across users, render those statically (or via ISR) and reserve SSR only for the genuinely per-user holes — ideally with Partial Prerendering.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An optimization of an SSR route that is dynamic for good reason but too slow.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Whole-page SSR blocks the response on all data, even data that could be static or streamed.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Streaming sends the shell first; caching and PPR limit per-request rendering to the personalized portions only.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows you can preserve correctness (personalization) while applying the right freshness/perf trade-offs — exactly the judgment SSR questions probe.

nestedTopics.title: Streaming with Suspense
nestedTopics.explanation: Send the static shell immediately and stream slow/dynamic sections as they resolve.

nestedTopics.title: Partial Prerendering
nestedTopics.explanation: Serve a static shell from the CDN while server-rendering only the dynamic holes.

followUps.question: What signals tell you a route shouldn't be fully SSR?
followUps.answer: Most of the page is identical across users, the dynamic data is a small slice, or the build output marks an unexpectedly large route as dynamic.

coding.question: Write an App Router page that renders per request and greets the current user, reading the session cookie and fetching fresh data.
coding.thoughtProcess: I need the route to be dynamic. Reading cookies() is a dynamic function, which alone forces SSR. I'll fetch the user with cache: 'no-store' so it's always fresh, pass the session along, and render the name. No getServerSideProps is needed in the App Router.
coding.lineByLine: Importing and calling cookies() reads request-only data, which makes Next.js render the route dynamically per request. The fetch uses cache: 'no-store' so the user data is never cached and reflects the current request, and forwards the session cookie for auth. The component returns HTML embedding the per-user data, which the server renders and streams.
coding.timeComplexity: N/A — a rendering strategy, dominated by the upstream fetch latency.

alternativeApproaches.title: Explicit route config
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Force the whole route dynamic regardless of fetch caching.

followUps.question: What if you also need a piece of cacheable data on this page?
followUps.answer: Fetch the shared data with default/forced caching (or revalidate) and stream it; only the no-store/cookie-dependent parts force per-request rendering.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Reserve SSR for routes whose output genuinely depends on the request (auth/session, live data, request headers). Keep the bulk of a page static where possible and isolate the dynamic portions behind Suspense boundaries; with Partial Prerendering you can serve a static shell from the CDN and server-render only the dynamic holes.
productionDeepDive.performance: SSR's cost is per-request render latency plus compute. Stream with Suspense so the shell paints first, cache any sub-fetches that aren't request-specific, and keep Client Components small to limit hydration JS. Profile TTFB and avoid blanket no-store on data that could be cached.
productionDeepDive.security: SSR keeps data access, database calls, and secrets on the server; never expose tokens to Client Components. Authorize inside server code/route handlers and validate the session on every request, since the page is rendered per request anyway.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Each SSR request consumes server resources, so SSR scales with capacity, not for free like CDN static pages. Isolate expensive SSR routes, add request-level caching where safe, and use autoscaling; consider moving shareable content to SSG/ISR to shed load.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Make a route's dynamic nature explicit (force-dynamic or a clear comment) so reviewers understand why it isn't static. Centralize session/cookie reads and document any no-store fetches so accidental dynamic rendering is easy to spot.
productionDeepDive.observability: The build output marks each route static (○) or dynamic (ƒ/λ); watch for routes unexpectedly flipped to dynamic. Monitor TTFB, error rates, and server CPU per SSR route, and trace slow upstream fetches that inflate per-request latency.

caseStudies.problem: Pages must reflect the logged-in user and live inventory, so they can't be statically pre-built.
caseStudies.solution: Render those routes with SSR (cookies + no-store fetches) and stream the static shell while personalized sections load.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Higher TTFB and per-request compute versus static pages, mitigated by streaming and caching shareable data.
caseStudies.lessons: Use SSR only for the genuinely per-request slice and keep everything else static to control cost and latency.

A live activity feed fetches with no-store so it's always current

Cache shareable sub-fetches to cut per-request work

How would you reduce its TTFB without losing personalization?

keyTakeaways: SSR renders a route's HTML on the server on every request, embedding live, possibly per-user data — fresh, personalized, secure, and SEO-friendly.
In the App Router there's no getServerSideProps: a route becomes SSR via an uncached fetch (no-store), a dynamic function (cookies/headers/searchParams), or export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'.
SSR's cost is higher TTFB and per-request server compute; SSG/ISR serve faster and cheaper from a CDN but can't be fresh per request.
Reserve SSR for genuinely request-dependent content; keep the rest static and stream the shell to minimize the dynamic work.
SSR keeps secrets and data access on the server — never ship tokens to Client Components.
